title: "9 · Introduction to neural networks"

Neural networks attract attention out of proportion to how often they are the right
choice. The mechanics are less mysterious than the reputation suggests: a network is
a stack of simple weighted sums with a nonlinearity between them, trained by the same
gradient descent introduced in
[4 · How algorithms learn](../04-how-algorithms-learn/index.qmd).

They shine on data with structure a person cannot easily summarise into features —
images, audio, video. Marine science has plenty of that: benthic imagery, echosounder
returns, whale call recordings. For a table of environmental covariates with a few
thousand rows, a boosted tree will usually match or beat a network with a fraction of
the effort and far more interpretability.

This section covers what they are, and gives you a basis for deciding you do not need
one.

## In this section

- Neurons, layers, weights, and activation functions
- Forward propagation and backpropagation
- Loss functions and gradient descent
- Strengths, limitations, and data requirements
- When neural networks are — and are not — appropriate
